newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Cold War remembered as Hanoi blasts U.S. radio.
newsitem.headline: Cold War remembered as Hanoi blasts U.S. radio.

text.p: Hanoi blasted the United States on Tuesday in a furious tirade against plans by U.S. station Radio Free Asia to begin broadcasts to the region in Vietnamese.

A signed and lengthy commentary in the official Quan Doi Nhan Dan (People's Army) newspaper accused Washington of seeking to undermine stability in Asia, but also exposed deeper sores from a war that ended nearly 22 years ago.
"You (the United States) should know that for the Vietnamese people, for a long time, whenever the adjective 'Free' is used by you it implies no beautiful meaning," it said.

"The Vietnamese people don't want to repeat that whenever the adjective 'Free' has been applied to us by you, it's linked with 'free aggression', 'freely bombing', 'freely spraying toxic chemicals', 'freely killing and jailing patriotic people', 'freely distorting the truth'...and 'freely interfering in the internal affairs of sovereign countries,'" it said.

The newspaper added that by pushing ahead with the station, Washington was demonstrating a continued Cold War ambition to defeat communism and a willingness to violate the principles of respect for other nations' independence.

Vietnam has lashed out at plans for Radio Free Asia -- known officially as the Asia Pacific Network -- on several occasions, but Tuesday's commentary was directed squarely at Washington, warning of the impact on relations between the former foes.

It described the station's purpose as blunt interference in the internal affairs of sovereign countries in Asia and warned that the United States would succeed only in stirring animosity in the region.
Hanoi and Washington normalised diplomatic ties in 1995, two decades after the war ended with the collapse of U.S.-backed South Vietnam to the forces of the communist North.
Relations have progressed slowly since then, and the two countries have yet to achieve full economic and trade normalisation.
